core: Working definition (attributed): water-soluble vitamins are vitamins that dissolve in water and are not stored in large amounts; MedlinePlus describes the water-soluble vitamins (C and the B vitamins) as dissolving in water with leftover amounts leaving in urine, and OpenStax states they are dissolved in water with excess intake excreted in urine

The two families: the B vitamins and vitamin C; the B vitamins share a job as coenzymes assisting the enzymes that metabolize carbohydrates, fats, and proteins; vitamin C is required for collagen synthesis and plays a role in immune function

Named individuals: B12 (cobalamin) helps keep nerve cells healthy and is needed to form red blood cells, with natural food sources limited to animal foods; folate is needed to form DNA and new cells including red blood cells; vitamin C cannot be made by humans and is needed for collagen and wound healing
How they travel: absorbed with water into the bloodstream; excess mostly passes in urine
Why regular intake matters: the body does not store them in large amounts, so a skipped day is simply missing; vitamin B12 is the known exception, stored in the liver for years

Deficiency signs: fatigue and anemia; megaloblastic anemia is the primary clinical sign of folate or vitamin B12 deficiency; vitamin C deficiency can cause anemia, and severe shortage causes scurvy characterized by fatigue

Food sources: fruits (citrus, kiwifruit, strawberries), vegetables (dark green leafy vegetables, peppers, broccoli, brussels sprouts), grains (listed among folate sources; enriched grains fortified with folic acid since 1998), meat and fish (vitamin B12), and dairy and eggs (vitamin B12)
Honest framing: water-soluble vitamins are the daily mail, not the warehouse; no dosing advice given
supporting: B12 storage magnitude: the body stores about 1 to 5 mg, roughly 1,000 to 2,000 times a typical daily intake, so deficiency symptoms can take years to appear
Humans cannot synthesize vitamin C endogenously, unlike most animals, so it is an essential dietary component
All food examples for individual vitamins are original to this lesson (salmon, milk, eggs; spinach, asparagus, lentils; oranges, peppers, kiwifruit)

claims.claim: Water-soluble vitamins are vitamins that dissolve in water and are not stored in large amounts; OpenStax states they are dissolved in water and that excess intake is excreted in urine, and MedlinePlus describes the water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and the B vitamins) as dissolving in water with leftover amounts leaving the body in urine.

The water-soluble vitamins consist of two families, the eight B vitamins and vitamin C; the B vitamins act as coenzymes that assist the enzymes metabolizing carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, while vitamin C is required for collagen biosynthesis and plays a role in immune function.

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) helps keep nerve cells healthy and is needed to form red blood cells; natural food sources of vitamin B12 are limited to animal foods, and the body stores about 1 to 5 mg (roughly 1,000 to 2,000 times a typical daily intake), so deficiency symptoms can take years to appear.

Folate, the natural food form of vitamin B9, is needed to form DNA and new cells, including red blood cells; spinach, liver, asparagus, and brussels sprouts are among the foods with the highest folate levels, and folate sources include vegetables, fruits and fruit juices, nuts, beans, peas, seafood, eggs, dairy products, meat, poultry, and grains.

Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin humans cannot synthesize, so it is an essential dietary component; it is required for collagen biosynthesis, which plays a vital role in wound healing, and the best food sources are fruits and vegetables, especially citrus fruits, red and green peppers, kiwifruit, broccoli, strawberries, and brussels sprouts.

Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in the watery contents of the digestive tract and are absorbed with water, then carried in the bloodstream; blood carries vitamins and salts from the gut to the liver. Excess intake of water-soluble vitamins is excreted in the urine, and unused amounts are lost primarily through urine.

Because water-soluble vitamins are not stored in large amounts, regular intake matters: a water-soluble vitamin not obtained today is not available tomorrow. Vitamin B12 is the known exception because the liver stores years' worth.

General deficiency signs of the water-soluble family include fatigue and anemia: fatigue is listed among the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency and of folate deficiency, megaloblastic anemia is the primary clinical sign of folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, vitamin C deficiency can cause anemia, and severe vitamin C shortage causes scurvy characterized by fatigue.

Food groups that supply water-soluble vitamins include fruits (citrus, kiwifruit, strawberries), vegetables (dark green leafy vegetables, peppers, broccoli, brussels sprouts), grains (listed among folate sources, and enriched grains have been fortified with folic acid since 1998), meat and fish (vitamin B12), and dairy and eggs (vitamin B12).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether water-soluble vitamins are stored at all
positions: Popular framing sometimes says water-soluble vitamins are not stored at all
Authoritative sources say they are not stored in large amounts and name vitamin B12 as the stored exception (about 1,000 to 2,000 times a typical daily intake held in the liver)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches not stored in large amounts with vitamin B12 as the named exception, matching NIH ODS and MedlinePlus.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether extra water-soluble vitamins are a useful reserve
positions: Product marketing implies extra water-soluble vitamins build a helpful reserve
Sources: excess mostly passes in urine, so extra intake does not build a reserve for later
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the elimination fact and gives no dosing or supplement advice; supplements belong to the supplements topic.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamin B12 - Health Professional Fact Sheet
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: natural food sources of vitamin B12 are limited to animal foods (meat, fish, poultry, dairy, eggs); the body stores about 1 to 5 mg (about 1,000 to 2,000 times a typical daily intake), so deficiency symptoms can take several years to appear; vitamin B12 deficiency can cause fatigue, neurological changes, and megaloblastic anemia.

sourceRecords.title: Folate - Health Professional Fact Sheet
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: folate is a water-soluble B vitamin naturally present in foods; folate is needed for DNA formation and cell division; megaloblastic anemia is the primary clinical sign of folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, with symptoms including weakness, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating; spinach, liver, asparagus, and brussels sprouts are among the foods with the highest folate levels; folate sources include vegetables, fruits, beans, dairy, meat, poultry, and grains; enriched grain products have been fortified with folic acid since 1998.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamin C - Health Professional Fact Sheet
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble vitamin that humans cannot synthesize, making it an essential dietary component; it is required for collagen biosynthesis, and collagen plays a vital role in wound healing; insufficient vitamin C intake causes scurvy, characterized by fatigue or lassitude and connective tissue weakness; best sources are fruits and vegetables, especially citrus fruits, red and green peppers, kiwifruit, broccoli, strawberries, and brussels sprouts.
